title: Microrheological and Microfluidic Approaches for Evaluation the Mechanical Properties of Blood Cells
content: Microfluidics has become an important field for studying blood microrheology and the mechanical properties of blood cells - erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets. Alterations in hemorheological properties in patients with diabetes, hypertension, obesity, sickle cell anaemia, cerebrovascular and peripheral vascular diseases are related to an increase in blood viscosity and red blood cells (RBCs) aggregation and a decrease in RBC deformability. Hemorheological disturbances are crucial in the impairment of microcirculation and microvascular perfusion. In blood vessels, impaired hemorheological parameters in patients can lead to increased resistance to blood flow, increased forces on the endothelial wall, and microvascular disorders. Erythrocyte deformability is a potential biomarker for diseases such as diabetes, malaria, and cancer. This work reviews recent developments in microfluidic technologies for in vitro assays of erythrocyte (RBC) deformability and aggregation, leukocyte aggregation and adhesion. The study summarises the key principles of microfluidic platforms and the experimental results obtained for hemodynamic parameters such as erythrocyte deformability, aggregation, leukocyte aggregation and adhesion. The advantages and limitations of each technique are reviewed and discussed. Future research opportunities for improving the devices are analysed. Some aspects of modelling microrheological properties are addressed. The devices and experimental systems developed are promising tools for studying erythrocyte deformability and aggregation, and leukocyte adhesion.
